name: Speech recognition and voice command
definition: A machine that recognizes spoken words and carries out spoken commands, such as voice-operated doors or computers.
what: Apple launched the iPhone 4S with Siri, putting spoken commands in the hands of ordinary phone users.

sources.title: Siri
sources.quote: On October 14, 2011, Apple launched the iPhone 4S with a beta version of Siri.

note: The first pass gave 2011-10-04, which is the announcement; the iPhone 4S went on sale 14 October 2011. Earlier but narrower mass uses: telephone call-routing by voice (AT&T 1992), DragonDictate/NaturallySpeaking for PC users (1990s) were niche, not routine for ordinary people.

name: Automatic dictation transcription
definition: A machine that listens to dictation and produces the written or typed text automatically.
what: IBM's Tangora, a voice-activated typewriter handling a 20,000-word vocabulary, built by Fred Jelinek's team.

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: By the mid-1980s, Fred Jelinek's team at IBM created a voice-activated typewriter called Tangora, which could handle a 20,000-word vocabulary.

note: Year is only 'mid-1980s' in the source; 1985 is an approximation. Almost certainly too late: RCA's Olson and Belar built an experimental 'phonetic typewriter' that typed from speech and published it in J. Acoust. Soc. Am. in 1956 (found via search; I could not fetch a page to quote, so not used). That earlier prototype, limited to a single talker and a small phoneme set, is the likely true first demonstration.

name: Automatic dictation transcription
definition: A machine that listens to dictation and produces the written or typed text automatically.
what: Dragon Dictate released as a consumer dictation product (discrete words, DOS).

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: 1990 – Dragon Dictate, a consumer product released in 1990.

note: First pass said 1997 NaturallySpeaking, which was the first continuous-speech product, not the first dictation product. The same Wikipedia list gives 1987 'a recognizer from Kurzweil Applied Intelligence' (Kurzweil's medical-report dictation system); the line has no detail, so I could not confirm it as dictation and kept 1990. An earlier 1987 or 1984-85 product may fit. No mass_adoption sourced: dictation by speech only became routine on smartphones in the 2010s, but no fetched source states it.

name: Speech synthesis
definition: A machine that generates spoken language with an artificial voice, such as a talking computer reading out answers.
what: Telesensory Systems' Speech+ talking calculator for the blind, with a synthesized voice, was in use; the Kurzweil Reading Machine for the Blind (Votrax synthesizer) appeared in the same year.

sources.title: Speech synthesis
sources.quote: One of the first was the Telesensory Systems Inc. (TSI) Speech+ portable calculator for the blind in 1976.

note: Earlier systems existed (Umeda's 1968 text-to-speech, MUSA 1975 reading Italian) but I found no evidence they were used outside the lab. Voder (1939) and Kempelen's machine were exhibitions. Date 1976 is the source's year for 'one of the first' handheld devices; a slightly earlier use is possible.

name: Speech synthesis
definition: A machine that generates spoken language with an artificial voice, such as a talking computer reading out answers.
what: Siri on the iPhone 4S brought a talking computer that answers aloud to ordinary phone users.

sources.title: Siri
sources.quote: On October 14, 2011, Apple launched the iPhone 4S with a beta version of Siri.

note: Judgment call. Earlier mass-market talking devices: Texas Instruments Speak & Spell (1978) and talking games and chess computers (1979-80), which had voices but little routine use as 'answering computers'. Wikipedia source supports the date of launch, not the synthesis itself.

name: Conversational natural-language computer
definition: A computer that holds a conversation in ordinary human language, understanding questions and replying in kind.
what: OpenAI released ChatGPT; it reached 100 million users in two months.

sources.title: ChatGPT
sources.quote: ChatGPT gained one million users in five days and 100 million in two months.

note: Earlier mass-market assistants (Siri 2011, Alexa 2014) took commands and short questions rather than holding conversations; chatbots such as SmarterChild (2001) were popular but I did not source them. No first_practical_use is given: no fetched source identifies an out-of-lab deployment before the 1990s and I could not settle it.

name: Machine translation
definition: A machine that automatically translates written or spoken language from one human language into another.
what: Georgetown University and IBM translated more than sixty Russian sentences into English automatically on an IBM 701.

sources.title: Georgetown-IBM experiment
sources.quote: The Georgetown–IBM experiment was an influential demonstration of machine translation, which was performed on January 7, 1954.

sources.title: Machine translation
sources.quote: A demonstration was made in 1954 on the APEXC machine at Birkbeck College

note: The 1954 Birkbeck APEXC demonstration (rudimentary English to French; day not given) is the same year and I cannot tell which came first, so the Georgetown date is kept. Mid-1930s patents by Artsrouni (mechanical bilingual dictionary on punched tape) and Troyanskii were proposals or a word-lookup aid, not demonstrated translation. The system was a small demonstration (250 words, six rules).

name: Machine translation
definition: A machine that automatically translates written or spoken language from one human language into another.
what: IBM's Automatic Language Translator (AN/GSQ-16) was installed at the US Air Force Foreign Technology Division to convert Soviet technical documents to English.

sources.title: AN/GSQ-16 Automatic Language Translator
sources.quote: The translator was installed in 1959, dramatically upgraded in 1964, and was eventually replaced by a mainframe running SYSTRAN in 1970.

note: Single Wikipedia source. Another source (a 1997 NAIC paper, found by search, not fetched) says the Mark II system was installed at Wright-Patterson in 1964 as one of the first operational MT systems, so the 1959 installation may have been a pre-operational version. Other early uses I did not verify: Georgetown/Euratom/Atomic Energy Commission systems in the early 1960s; METEO weather-bulletin translation (1970s).

name: Machine translation
definition: A machine that automatically translates written or spoken language from one human language into another.
what: AltaVista Babel Fish (SYSTRAN) offered free web translation to the public and handled about 500,000 requests a day.

sources.title: Machine translation
sources.quote: AltaVista Babelfish, which racked up 500,000 requests a day (1997)

note: First free web translation was SYSTRAN's 1996 offering; 1997 is when it reached large daily use. Google Translate (April 2006) later brought it to hundreds of millions. 'Routine' use by ordinary people is arguable for 1997; a later date (2006) could also be argued.

name: Machine-generated writing
definition: A computer that composes stories, articles, poems or books automatically.
what: Environment Canada deployed FoG, which generated weather forecasts in English and French from data automatically.

sources.title: Natural-language generation
sources.quote: The earliest such system to be deployed was FoG, which was used by Environment Canada to generate weather forecasts

note: Source says only 'early 1990s'; 1990 is a placeholder year. Literature I recall gives about 1992 but I did not source it. Later: Reuters Tracer and the Associated Press / Los Angeles Times Quakebot (2014). Earlier practical text generation (e.g. form-letter mail merge) is a template fill, not composition. Eureka (1845) was a paid exhibition, not a practical tool.

name: Machine-generated writing
definition: A computer that composes stories, articles, poems or books automatically.
what: ChatGPT made automatic writing of text available to ordinary users, reaching 100 million users in two months.

sources.title: ChatGPT
sources.quote: ChatGPT gained one million users in five days and 100 million in two months.

note: Earlier mass exposure was to machine-written news snippets (AP earnings and sports reports since 2014) that readers did not choose or operate; ChatGPT is when ordinary people used machine writing routinely themselves.

name: Machine learning
definition: A machine that improves its performance from experience or data instead of being explicitly programmed for each task.
what: Marvin Minsky and Dean Edmonds built SNARC at Princeton (funding summer 1951), a neural-net machine that learned by reinforcement to solve a maze.

sources.title: Stochastic neural analog reinforcement calculator
sources.quote: They tested the machine on a copy of Shannon's maze, and found that it could learn to solve the maze.

note: Candidates: Ashby's Homeostat (1948, adapts to disturbances; closer to self-regulation than learning from experience), Shannon's Theseus maze mouse (1950; relays remember the maze path, and whether it 'learned' is disputed), Samuel's checkers program (begun 1949, first ran 1952, paper 1959; 'machine learning' coined 1959) and Rosenblatt's perceptron (1957-58). SNARC is a simulated maze solved by reinforced weights, so I take it as the earliest clear case, but this is a judgment and the date is only the year. Page for Theseus could not be fetched. No first_practical_use or mass_adoption given: ADALINE (1960) adaptive filters and later uses were not sourced, and 'routine' consumer use is too diffuse to date.
